q: Does the energy-conserving split (Eq. 5 field-parallel velocity correction) remain exactly conservative in a relativistic/electromagnetic PIC context where the velocity update is Lorentz-factor coupled and the potential term q*Phi is replaced by the full electromagnetic four-potential contribution?
basis: The paper (Sec 3.1, Eqs 4-5) derives the parallel-velocity correction in an electrostatic, non-relativistic setting inside a single element with constant E. Aleph as described is electrostatic; relativistic/EM extension is not addressed. Independent conservation checks reproduced the electrostatic invariants to machine precision but did not exercise Lorentz-factor coupling.
next_steps: Re-derive the split-child velocity equation replacing (1/2) m v^2 with (gamma-1) m c^2 and q*Phi with q*(Phi - v dot A/c); implement in a stand-alone Boris-pusher test with a prescribed EM field gradient; measure relative energy error across the same 20000-split sweep at gamma values 1.0, 1.1, 2.0, 10.0 to see whether the naive electrostatic form leaks energy in the relativistic regime and, if so, quantify the leak scaling.

q: How does the reweighting scheme interact with adaptive mesh refinement (AMR)? Specifically, does the element-local field assumption (constant E within an element used in the Eq-5 energy correction) still hold when children land in a newly-refined sub-element with a different local E, and does inter-level particle migration preserve the conservation invariants?
basis: Sec 3.1 uses a nearest-face bound dx_max and assumes constant E within the parent's element. Aleph as tested is uniform-mesh; AMR is not addressed in the paper. Our reimplementation used a single element and therefore did not stress the cross-element case.
next_steps: Build a two-level nested mesh test where a parent macroparticle sits near a refinement boundary; sweep child-displacement magnitudes so a fraction of children cross into the refined level with a different E; measure per-event energy error and count boundary-straddling events; propose either a bounded-dx-per-element policy or a re-evaluation of E along the child trajectory.

q: What is the GPU/exascale scaling behavior of the split/merge operators, and does the per-cell serialization implied by the pairwise merge (Eq 6-12 needs nearest-speed pairing within a cell) become the throughput bottleneck at Aleph scales targeted by Sandia/NVIDIA?
basis: The author list includes NVIDIA and the paper title claims performance, but the paper focuses on physics correctness rather than a GPU strong/weak scaling study. No throughput numbers are reproduced in the provided text for a multi-GPU or multi-node run, and Aleph internals are not public.
next_steps: Prototype the merge kernel in CUDA or SYCL with three pairing strategies (per-cell nearest-speed serial, atomic-buffered pairwise, and approximate bucketed pairing); benchmark on a single H100 at particle counts 1e6, 1e7, 1e8 per rank; measure occupancy and pair-search latency; compare against the split kernel throughput to identify the actual bottleneck.

q: How sensitive are the physical outputs (VDF shape, ionization rate, wall heat flux) to the chosen merge cutoffs (Eq 9: delta_v less than v_thermal, alpha less than 30 degrees) and to the split/merge target-weight window (W_min, W_max)?
basis: The paper fixes cutoffs at v_thermal at T=5 eV and 30 degrees and gives no sensitivity sweep. Our reimplementation recovered the KE-loss statistics (median 0.062 percent) at these fixed values only, so the sensitivity envelope of the method is unknown.
next_steps: In the 0D swarm test, sweep the angular cutoff over 10, 20, 30, 45, 60 degrees and the speed cutoff over 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 times v_thermal; measure fitted beta, EEDF second moment, and cumulative merge-KE-loss; identify the largest cutoff window that keeps thermal-energy drift below a stated tolerance (e.g. 1 percent per e-fold of growth).

q: How does the split/merge scheme compare quantitatively against alternative macroparticle coalescence approaches (e.g. Lapenta-Brackbill v-space Voronoi merging, Assous k-means merging, or the Welch-Rose weighted-density resampling) on the same 0D H2 growth test and Test-4.1 sheath problem?
basis: The paper motivates the method as an improvement over prior schemes but the extracted text does not include a head-to-head numerical benchmark against a named alternative. Our reimplementation only tested the paper's own scheme against its own invariants.
next_steps: Implement one alternative (Lapenta-Brackbill Voronoi merge is the smallest lift) in the same reimplementation harness; run both schemes on the identical 0D growth test at N_c in 100, 1000, 10000 with matched cutoffs where possible; report side-by-side fitted-beta bias, computational-count bounds, cumulative KE drift, and per-event cost; publish the harness so third parties can drop in additional schemes.
